forbidden_claims.statement_nl: Let [n choose k]_q denote the Gaussian q-binomial coefficient. Prove that for all integers n, k, ℓ with 0 ≤ k, ℓ ≤ n, if [n choose k]_q / [n choose ℓ]_q is a polynomial in q, then it has only nonnegative coefficients.

payload.role_in_assembly: Supplies nonzeroness and the exact degree formulas for the reduced numerator and denominator.

domain_restrictions: n and r must be integers.
The inequality 0 <= r <= n is required.
The quantity n - r is therefore a nonnegative integer.
The product defining (q;q)_m uses m as a nonnegative integer.
The claim is about a polynomial in the indeterminate q with coefficients in the integers.
semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For every pair of integers n and r satisfying 0 <= r <= n, the expression (q;q)_n divided by the product of (q;q)_r and (q;q)_{n-r} is a well-defined nonzero polynomial in Z[q], and its degree as a polynomial in q is r times (n - r).
quantifier_order: For all integers n and r, if 0 <= r <= n, then the stated property holds for the polynomial in q defined by the given formula.

payload.statement_nl: For all integers n and r with 0 <= r <= n, the Gaussian q-binomial coefficient [n choose r]_q := (q;q)_n / ((q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r}), where (q;q)_m := product_{i=1}^m (1 - q^i) and (q;q)_0 := 1, is a nonzero polynomial in Z[q] of degree r(n-r).

result_payload.proof_nl:
Let G_{n,r}(q) denote the displayed quotient G_{n,r}(q) := (q;q)_n / ((q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r}). For each m >= 0, (q;q)_m is a product of factors 1 - q^i, each nonzero in Z[q], so (q;q)_m is nonzero. Hence G_{n,r}(q) is at least a well-defined rational function.

We prove by induction on n that for every r with 0 <= r <= n, G_{n,r}(q) is a nonzero polynomial in Z[q] and deg G_{n,r}(q) = r(n-r).

Base case n = 0: then r = 0, and G_{0,0}(q) = 1. This is a nonzero polynomial of degree 0 = 0(0-0).

Inductive step: assume the claim holds for n-1, and let 0 <= r <= n. If r = 0 or r = n, then G_{n,0}(q) = (q;q)_n / ((q;q)_0 (q;q)_n) = 1 and similarly G_{n,n}(q) = 1. So these are nonzero polynomials of degree 0 = r(n-r).

Now assume 1 <= r <= n-1, so r-1 and n-r-1 are nonnegative. From the product definition, for every m >= 1 we have (q;q)_m = (1 - q^m)(q;q)_{m-1}. Therefore
G_{n-1,r}(q) = (q;q)_{n-1} / ((q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r-1}) = (1 - q^{n-r})(q;q)_{n-1} / ((q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r}),
and
q^{n-r} G_{n-1,r-1}(q) = q^{n-r}(q;q)_{n-1} / ((q;q)_{r-1} (q;q)_{n-r}) = q^{n-r}(1 - q^r)(q;q)_{n-1} / ((q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r}).
Adding these identities gives
G_{n-1,r}(q) + q^{n-r} G_{n-1,r-1}(q) = ((1 - q^{n-r}) + q^{n-r}(1 - q^r))(q;q)_{n-1} / ((q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r}) = (1 - q^n)(q;q)_{n-1} / ((q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r}) = G_{n,r}(q).
So we have the recurrence
G_{n,r}(q) = G_{n-1,r}(q) + q^{n-r} G_{n-1,r-1}(q).

By the induction hypothesis, G_{n-1,r}(q) and G_{n-1,r-1}(q) are nonzero polynomials in Z[q]. Hence G_{n,r}(q), being their sum after multiplying one of them by q^{n-r}, also lies in Z[q]. Their degrees are
deg G_{n-1,r}(q) = r((n-1)-r) = r(n-r-1),
and
deg(q^{n-r} G_{n-1,r-1}(q)) = (n-r) + (r-1)((n-1)-(r-1)) = (n-r) + (r-1)(n-r) = r(n-r).
Since r >= 1, we have r(n-r-1) < r(n-r). Thus the second summand has strictly larger degree than the first, so the top-degree term cannot cancel. Therefore deg G_{n,r}(q) = r(n-r), and in particular G_{n,r}(q) is nonzero.

This completes the induction. Therefore for all integers n and r with 0 <= r <= n, the Gaussian q-binomial coefficient (q;q)_n / ((q;q)_r (q;q)_{n-r}) is a nonzero polynomial in Z[q] of degree r(n-r).
result_payload.proof_summary: Induct on n. The boundary cases r = 0 and r = n give value 1 immediately. For 1 <= r <= n-1, derive directly from the product definition the q-Pascal recurrence G_{n,r} = G_{n-1,r} + q^{n-r} G_{n-1,r-1}. By induction both summands are polynomials in Z[q]. Their degrees are r(n-r-1) and r(n-r), so the second is strictly larger; hence the sum is nonzero and has degree exactly r(n-r).

used_external_facts: Only elementary algebra facts about Z[q]: products of nonzero polynomials are nonzero, deg(q^m P) = m + deg P for nonzero P, and if deg A < deg B then deg(A + B) = deg B.
